1.pericope_label: In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple

schools.summary: Calvin reports the stronger view that this is really the beginning of the book and that an error was made in collecting the prophecies, on the ground that the prophet here declines the office, seems a novice, and says that he has now seen the Lord; he calls these reasons feeble, answering that a man so overpowered by an extraordinary vision might well forget he was a prophet, since there was no feeling in him that the presence of God did not overpower, so that like one who had lost his senses he plunged himself into darkness, or rather like one despairing of life chose to die, and the godly ought to be so affected when God gives them tokens of his presence. Gill gives the year in three reckonings, the fifty-second of the reign, the year 3246 from the creation, and, on a father’s authority, the year in which the founder of Rome was born, and reports that some take the death not literally but of the leprosy that struck the king when he tried to burn incense.

Henry gives two purposes for the vision, to confirm the prophet’s faith so that he might be satisfied of the truth of what was afterwards revealed, and to work upon his affections so that reverence might quicken him and fix him to his service, since those who teach others the knowledge of God ought to be well acquainted with him themselves; he notes that the vision is dated for the greater certainty of it, and makes the date preach, since when the breath of princes goes forth our comfort is that the Lord reigns for ever, the king dying while the God of that people still lives.

Clarke reports that most interpreters take this chapter for the first of Isaiah’s prophecies, since it seems to contain his designation to the office, but doubts it, since the prophet is said to have prophesied in the reign of Uzziah and to have written that king’s acts, since the phrase in the year that Uzziah died probably means after his death as the same phrase does of another king, and since the prophecies are not arranged in order of time, four earlier chapters seeming by internal marks to be older than the first. Wesley says the Lord seen is the Divine Majesty as he subsists in three persons, and that the train is a royal and judicial robe, since he is represented as a judge.

Ellicott puts the vision just before the king’s death, since the first year of his successor would have been the more natural formula afterwards, and allows that the narrative may have been written later and set here deliberately, so that readers might see what the prophet saw and find in the preceding chapters the development of what he had heard; he fills in the moment with twenty years of outward prosperity and much inward corruption, a king who had profaned the temple either just dead or dragging out the dregs of his leprous life in seclusion, and an earthquake that had left a vague sense of impending judgment, and thinks it significant that the prophet’s first work as a writer was the history of that reign.

debates: Is this chapter the first of Isaiah’s prophecies? Clarke doubts it and argues from the writing of the king’s acts and from the ordering of the book; Calvin reports the stronger claim that it is the true beginning and answers it from the effect of the vision on the man who saw it; Ellicott allows that it was written later and placed here on purpose.

Was the vision before or after the king’s death? Ellicott says before, since the first year of the successor would have been the natural formula afterwards; Clarke says after, on the analogy of the same phrase used of another king; Gill reports a reading that takes the death for the leprosy that shut him up.

Why was the vision given at all? Henry answers that it was to confirm the prophet’s faith and to work on his affections; Calvin adds that God meant in the person of his servant to strike a rebellious people with alarm.
outliers: Gill dates the vision three ways at once, by the year of the reign, by the year from the creation, and by the birth of the founder of Rome.
Ellicott reconstructs the moment from an earthquake that had terrified the city, a king dying of leprosy in seclusion, and twenty years of prosperity covering much corruption.
Calvin describes the prophet as one who, losing his senses before the presence of God, willingly plunged into darkness and chose of his own accord to die.
themes: a date that raises a question of order
the first of the prophecies or not
a king dying while God reigns
a man overpowered out of his office
a robe that fills the temple

2.pericope_label: Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings: and one cried unto another and said, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts, the whole earth is full of his glory: and the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke

schools.summary: Gill rejects three readings of the seraphim, that they are the Son and the Spirit, that they are the two Testaments, and that they are angels, which he calls the common interpretation, makes them ministers of the Gospel, and reports that Jewish commentators identify them with the living creatures of the other vision; he reports that some connect the shaking with the earthquake of that reign and answers with a rabbi that the moving was in the vision and not in fact. Calvin is drawn to the opinion that there were two seraphim, answering to the cherubim over the ark, but will not assert where Scripture is silent; he draws the lesson that the angels are set before us for imitation, since the holiest service we can render is praise; and he makes the noise a proof that the voice was not human, since no mortal voice can shake a building.

Clarke explains that the Hebrews mean by the feet the whole lower part of the body and that where robes reached the ground bare feet were thought indecent, supporting this from a traveller who saw an eastern king sitting cross-legged with his robe drawn over his unshod feet for decency; and he gives the antiphonal singing a history, running from the ode at the sea to the time of Ezra. Wesley keeps the name of the seraphim to its meaning of fire, standing for their nature or their fervent zeal, and calls the shaking a token of anger and the smoke, elsewhere a sign of acceptance, a sign of anger here.

Ellicott notes that this is the only passage where the seraphim appear among the host of heaven, the word elsewhere naming the fiery serpents of the wilderness, and finds here no trace of serpent form nor of the animal forms of the cherubim, the burning ones being in the likeness of men with six wings; he records the old distinction between seraphim that excel in love and cherubim that excel in knowledge and notes that it rests on the etymology; he allows that the threefold cry may mark the mode of utterance or may be the Hebrew idiom of emphasis by threefold iteration, and reports that later readers have found in it the glory of God in past and present and future or a faint foreshadowing of the Trinity, while insisting that historically it cannot be separated from the name of the Holy One of Israel; and on the smoke he offers both a figure of wrath answering the smoke on the mount and the incense-smoke that symbolises prayer, objecting to the second that censers would then have been mentioned. Keil and Delitzsch describe the vision as given to a waking man whose outer senses were suspended while an inner sense was opened, and hold that the throne is the heavenly original of the earthly temple, so that the prophet is carried up; they deny that the seraphim sang in concert and describe a continuous antiphon; and they render the shaken parts as the foundations of the thresholds rather than the lintels, supporting the word from a rabbinic use of it for a hand-mill frame.

debates: What are the seraphim? Ellicott finds them men in form with six wings and no trace of the serpent whose name they bear; Gill rejects the Son and Spirit, the two Testaments and the angels alike and makes them ministers of the Gospel; Wesley keeps them an order of holy angels named from fire.
How many were there? Calvin inclines to two, answering to the cherubim over the ark, but refuses to assert it where Scripture is silent, remembering that another prophet saw thousands of thousands.

What does the threefold holy signify? Ellicott offers the mode of utterance, the Hebrew idiom of emphasis, and the readings of later devotion that find the three tenses of God’s glory or a foreshadowing of the Trinity; Wesley takes it for the Trinity outright.
outliers: Clarke supports the covering of the feet from a traveller’s account of an eastern king seated cross-legged with his robe drawn over his unshod feet.
Keil and Delitzsch support their rendering of the thresholds from a rabbinic use of the same word for the frame of a hand-mill.
Ellicott weighs the smoke as either a figure of wrath or the incense of prayer, and rejects the second because censers are not mentioned.
themes: burning ones in the likeness of men
two seraphim or thousands
an antiphon that never breaks off
thresholds rather than lintels
smoke of wrath or of prayer

5.pericope_label: Then said I, Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips: then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand: and he laid it upon my mouth and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips, and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged

schools.summary: Calvin agrees with the rendering that makes the prophet dumb and wonders why one father rendered it otherwise, since the passive form is plainly marked; he observes that men imagine they live, swelled with vain confidence, because they do not know God, and that until he reveals himself we think ourselves not men but gods, true humility springing from the sight of him. On the coal he guards the transaction at both ends, since it had no virtue of its own, as superstitious men imagine of the magical arts, and the angel administered the cleansing without being its author, while the sign was still useful because we are not angels who can behold the mysteries of God unassisted; and he answers the objection that it is absurd to cleanse a tongue the Spirit had already used, since the Lord had cleansed him before by degree and this cleansing is greater because he meant to raise him to higher dignity. Gill allows that a good man may think himself miserable, partly for his own corruptions and partly for the company he keeps, and says that forgiving sin is God’s act alone while preaching forgiveness is the work of his ministers.
Henry is struck by the reversal, since one would have expected the man so favoured to call himself blessed, and instead he cries that he is a gone man, silenced, struck dumb.

Clarke will not have undone and renders it I am become dumb, from a root meaning to be silent, reporting that twenty-eight manuscripts, three editions, three old versions and some Jewish interpreters support the reading; he keeps to the altar of burnt-offering, on which the fire that first came down from heaven burned perpetually, and makes the coal the word of prophecy put into the prophet’s mouth. Wesley makes the prophet an unclean branch of an unclean tree, involved by omission and commission in the guilt of his people, and notes that the coal was laid so as to touch the lips and not to burn them.

Keil and Delitzsch give the reason for the terror, since the holiness of God is to a sinner a consuming fire and the distance between creature and Creator is of itself prostrating, as the seraphim showed by veiling their faces; they call the forgiveness a heavenly sacrament conveyed by a seraphic absolution, note that the flight of one implies a large and indefinite number, and leave open whether what was taken with the tongs was a red-hot stone or a burning coal. Ellicott sets the cry among its parallels and finds a contrast with the lawgiver, who felt chiefly the want of utterance where the thought here is of lips defiled by past sins of speech, unclean as the lips of one stricken with leprosy; he prefers to place the altar of incense beside the prophet rather than in heaven, so that what had seemed formal worship was quickened with living power and the symbol became sacramental, observes that fire is throughout the Bible the sign at once of wrath and love, and divides the absolution into pardon and purity.

debates: Does the prophet say that he is undone or that he is struck dumb? Clarke renders it dumb and reports manuscripts, editions, versions and interpreters in support; Calvin agrees and wonders at the other rendering, since the passive form is plainly marked.

Which altar did the seraph go to? Keil and Delitzsch take it for the heavenly original of the altar of incense; Ellicott prefers the earthly altar beside which the prophet stood, since on that reading the symbol became sacramental; Clarke keeps to the altar of burnt-offering with its perpetual fire.

What ailed the prophet’s lips? Ellicott contrasts him with the lawgiver, who wanted the gift of utterance, since here the lips are defiled by past sins of speech; Wesley adds the guilt of his people’s sins by omission and commission.
outliers: Calvin denies that the coal had any virtue of its own, as superstitious men imagine of the magical arts, and makes the angel the administrator but not the author of the cleansing.
Ellicott calls the moment a purgatory of instantaneous agony, fire being throughout the Bible the sign at once of wrath and of love.
Keil and Delitzsch infer from the flight of one seraph that their number was large and indefinite.
themes: a word that may mean dumb
the sight that shows a man what he is
a coal from which altar
a symbol quickened into a sacrament
pardon and purity together

8.pericope_label: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I, send me: and he said, Go and tell this people, Hear ye indeed but understand not, and see ye indeed but perceive not

schools.summary: Calvin asks why God should speak as though he could not find a qualified man, reports the view that this reproves the ignorance of the priests, and prefers to refer it to the certainty of the calling, since the deliberation shows the appointment was made by choice and not at random, God not hesitating but speaking so on our account; and he reads the warning of the ninth verse as armour, since the prophet needed fortifying like a brazen wall against a stubbornness he would meet for more than sixty years, and was bidden to teach without regard to the effect. Gill notes that one paraphrase makes the speaker the Word of the Lord rather than the Father.

Henry says God took the prophet at his word and sent him on a strange errand, to foretell the ruin of his people and even to ripen them for it, and counts the passage quoted or referred to six times in the New Testament, taking this to show that such spiritual judgments fall most often in gospel times and that, though they make the least noise, they are the most dreadful.

Wesley calls the change of number very remarkable and takes it to intimate a plurality of persons in the Godhead, and meets the difficulty of the imperative form in the ninth verse by making it not a command of what the people ought to do but a prediction of what they would do, their sin being their punishment, the word continuing while the Spirit is withdrawn, so that they shall be as unable as they are now unwilling to understand. Clarke contributes two manuscript variants and nothing more.

Ellicott says the cleansing has made the prophet one of the heavenly brotherhood, an angel called to an angel’s work; on the mixture of singular and plural he denies a plural of majesty, since the great kings of the east always spoke of themselves in the singular and that usage was the invention of a later and more servile court, allows that God is here a king in council, and holds that Christian thought has scarcely erred in finding a dim foreshadowing of a plurality within the Unity; and he calls the commission perhaps the hardest task ever given to a man, since ardent dreams of reformation were scattered and the prophet had to face a fruitless labour and the sense of increasing the evil he strove against, though supported by the knowledge that a remnant should be saved. Keil and Delitzsch refuse three explanations of the plural, self-consultation, majesty and abstraction, and refer it to the seraphim, who with the Lord form one deliberative body; and they put the paradox of the commission sharply, since the seraph absolved the prophet so that he might not absolve but harden his people by his word.

debates: What does the plural in the question mean? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both reject a plural of majesty, Ellicott because the great kings spoke of themselves in the singular; Keil and Delitzsch refer it to the council of seraphim, while Ellicott and Wesley find in it a foreshadowing of a plurality of persons.

Why does God deliberate at all? Calvin answers that the appointment was made by choice and not at random, and that God does not hesitate, such ways of speaking being used on our account; some, he reports, take it for a reproof of the ignorant priesthood.

How can the prophet be commanded to harden? Wesley makes the imperatives a prediction rather than a command; Keil and Delitzsch state the paradox that the absolved man is sent to harden; Calvin turns the warning into armour against sixty years of stubbornness.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch observe that the seraph absolved the prophet with the coal so that he might not absolve but harden his people by his word, the exact opposite of the mission he had just experienced.
Henry counts the passage quoted or referred to six times in the New Testament and infers that such judgments fall most often in gospel times.
Ellicott hears a touch of scorn in the phrase this people, and Keil and Delitzsch note that it points back to the people of unclean lips whom the Lord will not call his own.
themes: a man made fit for an angel’s work
singular and plural in one question
a deliberation held on our account
a commission to close the eyes
imperatives that are predictions

10.pericope_label: Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed. Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate

schools.summary: Gill offers three readings of making the heart fat, that the gospel does it through the wickedness of man’s heart and is a savour of death unto death to some as the sun hardens clay, or that the prophet is to declare their hearts already gross, or that God will give them up to a judicial hardness; and he takes the question how long to be asked of the blindness and impenitence. Calvin treats the passage as a doctrine of perpetual use, since the prophet is told beforehand that he will not merely labour fruitlessly but blind the people, and yet that these labours, bringing death and ruin, are an acceptable sacrifice; every faithful minister meets the same result, and Satan excites his followers to raise a dislike of instruction on the pretence that it is useless or injurious and that the world has grown worse by preaching. Calvin also makes the prayer a lesson in the twofold character a prophet must sustain, unshaken in proclaiming judgment yet not devoid of compassion for the brethren whose destruction his office obliges him to foretell, as Jeremiah first complained of his task and afterwards revived his courage.

Clarke insists the prophet speaks of the event and not of God’s purpose and act by his ministry, since prophets are elsewhere said to perform what they only foretell, one given a charge over nations to pluck up and pull down and another saying he came to destroy the city when he means he came to prophesy its destruction; he allows the plainer idiom, ye certainly hear but do not understand, and observes that hearing without understanding is a common saying in many languages, used by Demosthenes who expressly calls it a proverb and by Aeschylus, which the prophet raises into something with the air of poetry. He also reports a variant reading be left for be utterly desolate. Wesley ascribes the hardening to the prophet because God inflicted the judgment by his ministry, partly by foretelling what the preaching would produce and partly by withdrawing the light and help of his Spirit, so that they were made unable to see because they had first been unwilling; he calls the question an abrupt speech of great passion and astonishment and dates the desolation first by the Babylonians and afterward by the Romans.

Ellicott compares the hardening with that of Pharaoh and of Sihon, calls it the headstrong will that defies restraint, notes that the poets of Greece recognised a judicial blindness following on sinful deeds, and cites the mediaeval adage that whom God wishes to destroy he first drives mad while excluding the wishing to destroy by the clearer revelation of a God not willing that any should perish; he renders shut their eyes literally as daub or besmear, mentions a son of the Great Mogul punished that way by his father, and with Cheyne quotes Shakespeare on the wise gods sealing our eyes. On the question how long he hears what is ever on the lips of those facing the mystery of evil, cried again near the close of the exile and by the souls beneath the altar, and reads the answer as meeting the prophet within his own horizon, stroke after stroke until the sin has been adequately punished, though the darkness does not exclude a glimmer of eternal hope. Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet heard it with sighing and yet with obedience, and that the question was forced from him by sympathy with his own nation and warranted by the certainty that a God true to his promises could not cast off his people for ever.

debates: Is the prophet commanded to harden, or only to announce the hardening? Clarke says he speaks of the event and not of God’s purpose, prophets being said to perform what they foretell; Wesley ascribes it to the prophet because God inflicted it by his ministry and by withdrawing his Spirit; Gill allows all three, an effect of preaching, a declaration of fact, or a giving up to judicial hardness.

How far does God will the ruin? Ellicott accepts the mediaeval adage as one aspect of the law but strikes out the wishing to destroy as excluded by clearer revelation; Calvin holds that the blinding is foretold and yet that the ministry remains an acceptable sacrifice.

What warrants the question how long? Keil and Delitzsch say sympathy forced it from him, resting on the certainty that God could not cast off his people for ever; Calvin makes it the compassion proper to a prophet who must still proclaim judgment; Ellicott makes it the perennial question of those who face the mystery of evil.
outliers: Ellicott reads shut their eyes as literally to daub or besmear and points to a son of the Great Mogul blinded by his father as a punishment.
Clarke traces the saying about hearing and not understanding to Demosthenes, who calls it a proverb, and to Aeschylus, seeing they saw in vain and hearing they did not understand.
Calvin turns the fruitlessness into consolation, since the labour that brings death and ruin is still an acceptable sacrifice to God.
themes: a heart made fat by preaching
foretelling counted as performing
a judicial blindness known even to the poets
sympathy that forces a question
stroke after stroke, and a glimmer beyond

12.pericope_label: And the Lord have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land. But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof

schools.summary: Gill denies that the removal is to Babylon and refers it to the ends of the earth by means of the Romans, who were only instruments of a dispersion that was the Lord’s own doing and a judgment for sin; he reports the reckoning of ten kings from this death to the captivity, which Jarchi and Aben Ezra note and Kimchi lists from Jotham to Zedekiah, but since he takes the prophecy to respect the present dispersion rather than Babylon he reads the tenth as a remnant according to the election of grace, with the Targum agreeing. Calvin treats the twelfth verse as the eleventh restated, survivors of the war led into captivity and the land bereft, some fleeing, some banished, some perishing by the sword, the reward of obstinate men who add crime to crime until the indignation of God cannot be appeased. On the tenth he sets out both constructions, notes that the Hebrew forms differ only slightly, observes that the number of kings does run from Uzziah to Zedekiah and that naming them would support the prophet’s credit, and half prefers the reading in which the people keep a hidden vigour and sprout again like trees after winter, while expounding by the ten kings as the more probable.

Clarke holds that the accomplishment has made an obscure passage clear: when Nebuchadnezzar carried away the greater and better part, a tenth remained as vinedressers and husbandmen under Gedaliah and the dispersed gathered back to him, yet these fled into Egypt after his death against the warning God gave by Jeremiah and perished there; in the later completion the commonwealth was dissolved by the Romans, the nation grew numerous again out of the scanty residue left after the loss of above a million men, and Hadrian slew above half a million more and almost extirpated it again; and after all these destructions the stock still remains, from which God will cause his people to shoot forth again. He also passes on Kimchi’s explanation that the word means ten kings from the declaring of the prophecy. Wesley keeps the remnant indefinite, refers the return to the captivity in Babylon, reads two devourings, by the kings of Syria and afterwards by the Romans, and expects a further holy seed that shall look upon him whom they have pierced and mourn, the cast leaves concealing a vital principle that preserves life in the root and in due time sends it into all the branches.

Ellicott refers the removal to the policy of deportation adopted by the Assyrian kings and makes the verse programmatic, exile and return being the key-note of this prophet’s teaching from the first hour of his call and all his later work a development of that germ, the horizon widening until another empire than the Assyrian appears as the instrument of punishment; he renders a great forsaking as great shall be the deserted space and connects the words with what the prophet had heard from the lips of Micah. On the tenth he prefers, though there should be a tenth in it, yet this shall be again devoured with fire, a series of successive chastisements sifting the people till only the chosen remnant is left, the tenth being an ideally consecrated portion; he corrects teil tree to terebinth and the casting of leaves to being cut down, and finds in the stripped and lopped stump a stock from which a young shoot springs, holy because consecrated, carrying on the continuity of the nation’s life, the thought that governs the apostle’s hope that first the remnant and then all Israel should be saved, and which applied to the house of David becomes essentially Messianic. Keil and Delitzsch add only a technical footnote denying that the disputed word can mean plant, since of a tree deprived of its crown it can only mean the stump.

debates: To what removal do the words point? Gill refers them past Babylon to the dispersion by the Romans; Ellicott refers them to the deportation policy of the Assyrian kings, with the horizon later widening to another empire; Wesley leaves it at captivity in far countries.

What is the tenth? Gill and Wesley read a remnant, Gill according to the election of grace; Calvin reports and finally adopts the reading of ten kings from Uzziah to Zedekiah while owning that the other suits the imagery better; Clarke finds the tenth in the poor left in the land under Gedaliah.

Is the tenth a promise or another sentence? Ellicott insists on though there should be a tenth in it, yet this shall be again devoured, making it a further sifting before the remnant is reached; Gill, Wesley and Clarke take it straight as the surviving seed.
outliers: Clarke argues from the survival of the nation itself, through repeated destructions, that the stock still remains for God to make it shoot forth again.
Ellicott takes the tenth as an ideally consecrated portion and corrects teil tree to terebinth, reading the casting of leaves as being cut down.
Calvin notes that a prophet able to name how many kings would reign after his own death would gain no small credit for his doctrine.
themes: a dispersion counted as the Lord’s doing
a call whose germ is exile and return
ten kings or a remnant
a tenth devoured again
a stump with a vital principle in the root
